title: Supreme Court cancels Anand Mohan's early release in IAS officer's murder, orders him back to jail
dek: The court struck down Bihar's 2023 change to its prison rules that let the former MP walk free after 14 years, and told him to surrender within a month. Victims' families must now be heard before any remission.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The Supreme Court on Thursday set aside the premature release of former MP Anand Mohan, who was serving a life sentence for the 1994 killing of G. Krishnaiah, the district magistrate of Gopalganj in Bihar, and directed him to surrender to prison authorities within one month. If he does not, the authorities must take him into custody.

A bench of Justices Dipankar Datta and Sheel Nagu also struck down the Bihar government's 10 April 2023 amendment to its prison rules, which had removed a bar on early release for people convicted of murdering a public servant on duty and cleared the way for Mr Mohan to walk out of Saharsa jail that month. The court declared the amendment "unconstitutional, invalid and inoperative" and held that victims' families must be heard before a state decides to release a convict early, according to reports of the judgment.

## What the court decided

The case was a writ petition filed in 2023 by Telugu Umadevi Krishnaiah, known as Uma Krishnaiah, the slain officer's widow (W.P.(Crl.) No. 204 of 2023). The bench, which had reserved its verdict on 16 July, allowed the petition. Justice Datta read out the operative part of the judgment in court.

The main findings, according to reports of the judgment:

- The 2023 amendment to Rule 481(1)(a) of the Bihar Prison Manual, 2012 was "manifestly arbitrary and violative of Article 14". The court said the state had not shown a rational and legitimate public purpose for selectively deleting the category of murder of a public servant on duty, calling it a sudden departure from settled policy.
- The 24 April 2023 order granting Mr Mohan remission was "indefensible and unsustainable in law". Among other flaws, the remission board had relied on a 2021 opinion of the presiding judge instead of seeking a fresh, reasoned opinion, as Section 432 of the Code of Criminal Procedure requires.
- The sole test for early release cannot be that a convict "showed signs of reform".
- Victims or their families must be given a reasonable chance to make a representation before any premature release. Their objection, however, "would not confer any veto" over the state's decision.

> "Article 21 of the Constitution cannot be read as a one-sided guarantee." (Supreme Court judgment, as read out in court)

The bench said the right to life and liberty belonged not only to the convict but also to victims, their families and society, and that "the two rights of the victim as well as the convict have to be calibrated". "Judicial review is not an empty formality of supervision," it said.

The court did not close the door on Mr Mohan altogether. Bihar may consider his remission afresh under its rules, but only after he has surrendered or been taken into custody, and only after hearing Ms Krishnaiah. The court left open the wider legal question of whether a life convict can claim the benefit of a remission policy that is more generous than the one in force when they were convicted.

## Background

Krishnaiah, an IAS officer from what is now Telangana, was beaten to death by a mob in Muzaffarpur district in December 1994, when his official car tried to pass the funeral procession of a slain gangster, Chhotan Shukla. Mr Mohan, then an MLA, was leading the procession and was convicted of instigating the mob.

A trial court sentenced him to death on 5 October 2007. The Patna High Court commuted the sentence to rigorous life imprisonment on 10 December 2008, and the Supreme Court upheld that in July 2012.

Under Bihar's rules, people convicted of murdering a public servant on duty could not be considered for early release before serving 20 years. On 10 April 2023, the state's home department (prisons) amended the rule to delete that category. On the basis of a 20 April decision of the state's sentence remission council, the government then ordered the release of 27 life-term prisoners, including Mr Mohan, who had served about 14 years, according to reports at the time. He left Saharsa jail on 27 April 2023.

The decision drew sharp criticism. The Central IAS Association said at the time that changing the rules in a way that freed the convicted killer of a public servant on duty was "tantamount to denial of justice" and asked the state to reconsider, and IAS associations in several states objected too. Critics accused the then government of Chief Minister Nitish Kumar of changing the rules for political reasons. The state government has argued that the status of the victim cannot be a factor in denying remission.

Ms Krishnaiah moved the Supreme Court within days. In May 2023 the court issued notice and asked Bihar to produce the original records of the remission decision. During the hearings, the court asked how the murder of a public servant on duty was not treated as a "rarest of rare" case.

## What each side argued

Senior advocate Sidharth Luthra, for Ms Krishnaiah, argued that a life sentence means imprisonment for the rest of a convict's natural life and cannot be mechanically read as 14 years, that the remission board ignored relevant factors such as the prisoner's conduct and antecedents, and that the amendment was tailored to one man. "It is a case where this lady is battling against the travesty of justice," he told the court before it reserved judgment.

Bihar defended the release, arguing that Mr Mohan had served more than 14 years of actual sentence and was eligible under the rules as amended. Attorney General R. Venkataramani and senior advocate Ranjit Kumar appeared for the respondents.

No public response from Mr Mohan, his family or the Bihar government had been reported by Thursday afternoon.

## Why it matters

The ruling goes beyond one prisoner. Remission is decided by state governments, and the judgment sets out two rules every state will now have to follow: a change to remission policy must have a rational public purpose that the state can show in court, and the families of victims must be heard before a convict is freed early. Several other convicts, including politicians, were released under the same 2023 amendment, according to reports; the judgment's effect on their cases is not yet clear and was not spelt out in reports of the verdict.

The case also adds to a line of Supreme Court decisions scrutinising early releases, including its January 2024 judgment cancelling Gujarat's remission of the 11 convicts in the Bilkis Bano case.

## What happens next

- Mr Mohan has one month from Thursday, until about 26 December, to surrender. If he does not, prison authorities must arrest him.
- Bihar may begin a fresh remission process under its pre-2023 rules only after he is back in custody, and must give Ms Krishnaiah a hearing.
- The full text of the judgment is expected on the Supreme Court's website; this report is based on accounts of the verdict pronounced in court.
